headline: Nepal's Hidden Bird Finally Gets Its Moment
meta_description: A rare bird found only in Nepal is gaining attention after being spotted across all seven provinces for the first time.
summary_short: Nepal's mysterious spiny babbler, known to science for nearly 200 years, has now been documented in all seven provinces—but researchers say the world barely knows it exi…
body:
A small brown bird with distinctive black streaks has lived quietly in Nepal's shrublands for centuries, yet remains one of the world's least understood species. The spiny babbler, first scientifically described in 1836 by British naturalist Brian Houghton Hodgson, was long considered so rare that its existence seemed almost legendary. Then in June, ornithologists Hathan Chaudhary and Suraj Baral spotted it in Madhesh province, in Nepal's southern lowlands—a discovery that confirmed the bird now inhabits all seven of the country's provinces. More than 1,200 sightings have been recorded in the online database eBird, yet ornithologists still cannot explain why the spiny babbler exists nowhere else on Earth, nor do they fully understand its breeding patterns, population size, or how habitat loss and climate change affect it.

The bird's elusive nature reflects a larger conservation blind spot. Researchers like Kamal Raj Gosai at Kathmandu's Tri-Chandra Multiple Campus point out that endangered megafauna attract global attention and funding, while endemic species like the spiny babbler languish in obscurity. The real threat is immediate: Nepal's shrublands—the bird's preferred habitat—are vanishing as human settlements expand and communities convert them to agricultural land, mistaking them for wastelands. Between 1990 and 2010, shrublands in Kathmandu virtually disappeared entirely.

Yet hope lies in citizen science. Birdwatchers and enthusiasts across Nepal have been vital in documenting sightings, transforming a bird that was barely confirmed to exist outside Kathmandu gardens into a species with a documented range spanning mountains to lowlands. The spiny babbler's journey from obscurity reflects a simple truth: sometimes the most remarkable creatures are those waiting not to be discovered, but simply to be noticed.
quick_facts: First scientifically described in 1836, found only in Nepal
Spotted across all seven provinces for first time in June 2024
Elevation range: 443 to 2,135 meters depending on season
Over 1,200 sightings recorded in eBird database
Estimated 129 individuals in one research village
